# 06 — Fees and revenue

This page states the fee mechanics precisely, because vague fee language is how creators get
surprised.

## The pool fee is dynamic, and the hook is the policy

This is the fact most likely to be stale in anything you have read about this protocol before, so it
goes first.

Every launched project trades on one canonical Uniswap v4 pool, and that pool is initialized with
Uniswap's `DYNAMIC_FEE_FLAG`. The project's art hook returns a per-swap LP-fee override from
`beforeSwap`. The fee is therefore a function of **direction and time**, not a tier anybody picked:

- **Sell side: a flat base fee, forever**, at every instant of the pool's life including the first
  second.
- **Buy side: the same base fee**, unless the creator elected launch protection — in which case it
  starts far higher and decays to the base over the protection window. The whole schedule is in
  [12 — Launch protection](12-launch-protection.md).

An earlier generation of this protocol had a static fee and a hook with no fee path at all. If you
find a sentence in an old document saying the fee is static and the hook cannot override it, that
sentence is describing RC5.

**Consequence for interfaces: read the fee, do not print it.** A screen that hardcodes a number is
correct for a project that elected no protection and wrong for one that did, wrong for the first 98
minutes of every protected market, and unable to tell you which. Read `currentBuyFeePips()` /
`currentSellFeePips()` from the hook, recompute continuously in the browser, and show the direction
you are quoting.

There is exactly one place a fixed number is honest: the **base** fee, described as what the
schedule rests at rather than as what a trade costs right now.

### Uniswap's protocol fee is a separate charge

Uniswap governance can enable a protocol fee on any v4 pool through the `PoolManager`'s
`protocolFeeController`. That is Uniswap's mechanism, not the launchpad's: this protocol cannot
enable it, disable it, or receive it.

When one is live, v4 does not simply add the two — it compounds them:

```
swapFee = protocolFee + lpFee - floor(protocolFee * lpFee / 1_000_000)
```

State the two separately and never sum them into one number. They have two different recipients: the
LP fee accrues to the position (and divides creator/platform downstream), the protocol fee accrues to
Uniswap governance. A screen showing one total teaches a reader that the launchpad takes the whole
of it, which is false in both directions. And read the protocol fee from a live pool or report it as
unknown — on a pool that does not exist yet, "0%" is a claim about nothing.

## The split of collected LP fees

<!-- generated:fee-allocation -->
<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-doc-assets.mjs. Do not edit inside this block. -->

| Slice | Share of collected LP fees | Notes |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Creator entitlement | 75.00% | Claimed by the `ProjectRights` holder. Collaborator sub-splits come out of this share and can never reach the platform's. |
| $RELICS buy-and-entomb allocation | 12.50% | 50% of the platform share. |
| Retained protocol treasury | 12.50% | 50% of the platform share. |

These are ratios applied to **collected LP fees**, never to trading volume, and the settled figures differ by floor-division rounding. The declaration is `packages/project-schema/src/economics.js`; `npm run kit:economics` fails any second declaration of it.

<!-- /generated:fee-allocation -->

Two precision points that matter more than the percentages:

1. **The split applies to fees actually collected**, computed from the position's realized
   `BalanceDelta` — never from raw trade volume, never from token balances a contract happens to
   hold. The accounting takes amounts from the kernel rather than reading balances, so tokens
   donated to it raise a balance and change no ledger entry: a donation cannot inflate anyone's
   claim.
2. **75% of volume is not your revenue.** 75% of *collected LP fees* is. If Uniswap governance
   enables a protocol fee on your pool, the protocol fee is taken from the swap input before LP fee
   growth accrues, so the absolute fees your position earns per unit of volume fall — while the
   split of whatever *is* collected stays exactly the same.

Say: *"75% of collected LP fees."* Do not say: *"0.75% of all volume, forever."*

### Collaborator sub-splits

`LaunchParams.collaborators` is an array of `{ address recipient, uint16 bps }`. Those bps are a
fraction of **the creator's share only** — they can never reach the platform's — and they are set at
launch as part of the immutable fee policy.

The factory mints the rights token to itself, sets the collaborator splitter as the payout override,
and only then transfers the rights to the creator. The override deliberately survives a later
transfer: if it cleared, receiving your own rights would silently erase every collaborator's share.

### Inside the platform's share

The subdivision is a compile-time constant in the economic kernel with no setter. It resolves to a
50/50 split of the platform's own slice between the $RELICS buy-and-entomb allocation and the
retained protocol treasury — the two rows in the table above.

The technical statement is: **50% of the launchpad's net platform-fee revenue is allocated to $RELICS
buy-and-entomb.** Read that literally. It is *not* 50% of all trading fees, not 50% of creator fees,
not 50% of the pool fee, and not a Uniswap protocol fee.

The allocation is carved only from platform revenue. It never reads or touches a creator or
collaborator ledger, and the creator's share is untouched by this subdivision.

### Which asset the platform is paid in

The platform's share is denominated in the market's **selected quote**, and the 50/50 divides it
there — not in WETH. WETH is the special case, not the definition.

```
platform entitlement, in the SELECTED QUOTE
├─ retained treasury  → claimable IN THE QUOTE ASSET, immediately
└─ $RELICS allocation → QUOTE-denominated; becomes WETH only when an approved
                        route exists. Retryable. Never called settled until
                        WETH is actually received.
```

On a `PROJECT/USDG` market the protocol Safe claims USDG and the buy-and-entomb allocation holds USDG
waiting for a route. On a `PROJECT/WETH` market both halves are WETH the moment the split happens,
because there is nothing left to convert. On a BNB market the wrapped native is **WBNB** and both
statements above read with WBNB substituted — an interface that prints "WETH" there is naming the
wrong token.

Two things this does not change: the platform still takes no direct claim in your project token, and
the buy-and-entomb allocation still ends in $RELICS. It just gets there later — or, for some quotes,
not yet.

### Allocated is not spent

The nominal figures are ratios applied to collected LP fees. A buy-and-entomb half sitting in USDG is
*allocated*, not *spent*. Some quotes have no approved route at all, so an allocation can rest in
that asset indefinitely — which is a normal state with its own status, not an error and not a zero.

The public claim "50% of net platform revenue is allocated to $RELICS buy-and-entomb" stays true only
because a reader can see that *allocated* and *spent* are different words. Keep the quote-denominated
reserve in a field of its own, carrying the asset and its decimals, and leave the WETH field empty
until WETH arrives.

Nobody should promise that a fixed percentage of gross trading volume reaches either destination.
Volume is not fee revenue, and settlement is not free.

**Conversion costs fall only on the platform share, never on the creator's.** Getting the platform's
own slice from a project token into the quote, and from the quote into WETH, is the platform's
problem, paid out of the platform's own share. That guarantee is about the platform's own settlement
route; it does not extend to a conversion a creator elects — see `QUOTE_ONLY` below.

## What "buy-and-entomb" actually means

The buy-and-entomb executor spends tracked platform WETH to buy $RELICS on the one canonical
RELICS/WETH Uniswap v4 pool and sends **100% of the acquired $RELICS to the entombment address**, in
the same transaction. The tokens never sit with the executor, a treasury, or the caller.

Be exact about what that does:

- **Spendable and circulating supply fall.** The entombed $RELICS are at an address nobody controls
  and are unrecoverable.
- **`totalSupply` does not change.** $RELICS has **no burn function**; its total supply is a
  constant and always will be. A buy-and-entomb moves tokens; it does not shrink the ledger.
- **No ERC-20 burn event occurs.** There is no transfer-to-zero, no burn log, nothing an indexer
  could read as a supply decrease — because the deployed token has no supply-decreasing path at all.

All three have to be said together. "We burn $RELICS" on its own implies the supply number goes down,
and it does not. Say *buy-and-entomb*, *buyback and permanent removal*, or *permanently removes
purchased $RELICS from circulation*.

Buys are guarded: the executor anchors to its own TWAP oracle rather than spot price, bounds
deviation, caps each buy against live pool reserves, and reverts rather than accepting a partial
fill. A keeper calling it receives no $RELICS, chooses no recipient, and can only tighten the
minimum-out, never loosen it.

## Claiming your fees

Custody is split across a layer boundary, and the boundary is the whole safety argument.

**Principal lives in the immutable liquidity kernel** — code with no upgrade path, no withdrawal
function and no migration function. **Accounting lives in an upgradeable component** that holds no
position principal: what arrives there is the exact realized fee delta the kernel already took.

Stated plainly rather than dressed up: fees already sitting in the accounting layer are within reach
of an upgrade. Principal is not.

| Call | Who calls it | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `realizeFees(poolId)` | anyone | Realizes accrued fees at the kernel and records the split |
| `claimCreator(projectId)` | anyone (pays the creator) | Pays out the creator's accrued entitlement |
| `claimPlatformWeth(projectId)` | anyone (pays the platform) | Pays out the platform's accrued WETH |
| `convertCreatorTokenToWeth(...)` | anyone | Converts a `QUOTE_ONLY` creator's project-token entitlement |
| `convertPlatformTokenToWeth(...)` | anyone | Converts the platform's project-token share |

Read-only companions let a UI show pending amounts before anyone spends gas: `claimableCreatorWeth`,
`claimableCreatorToken`, `claimablePlatformWeth`, `platformTokenPending`,
`creatorTokenPendingConversion`.

Two callers are pinned and neither is the Safe: only the kernel may record fees, only the chain-local
factory may register a project. The Safe upgrades code and cannot record a fee or register a project.

## Which assets you are paid in

A v4 position earns fees on **both** sides of the pair, so a project's collected fees arrive as the
project token *and* the market's quote asset. What happens to the creator's half is elected at launch
and immutable afterwards:

<!-- generated:creator-payout -->
<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-doc-assets.mjs. Do not edit inside this block. -->

| Mode | Enum | What the creator claims |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `DUAL_ASSET` | 0 | The creator accrues and claims both real legs of their own pool: the project token and the selected quote asset, unconverted. |
| `QUOTE_ONLY` | 1 | The creator's own project-token entitlement is converted into THE PROJECT'S SELECTED QUOTE - not into WETH, unless WETH happens to be the quote. |

Elected once, at launch, and **immutable for the life of the project**. Never defaulted to QUOTE_ONLY. Converting a creator's fees without their say-so is not a default anyone may pick for them.
Both modes are available on both lanes, including the wrapped-native lane.

<!-- /generated:creator-payout -->

`QUOTE_ONLY` is **not** "WETH-only". The asset it settles in is whatever the market is quoted in: a
`PROJECT/USDG` market settles the creator in USDG, a `PROJECT/NVDA` market in NVDA, a `PROJECT/WETH`
market in WETH. Any interface that prints "WETH" for a quote-only market whose quote it has not read
is lying to the creator.

It also has a cost, and the cost is the creator's. `QUOTE_ONLY` is the creator's own swap through
their own pool: its execution cost — the pool fee and price impact — falls on the creator's
entitlement. The guarantee that conversion costs fall on the platform share covers the platform's own
settlement route and does not extend to a conversion a creator elects. Both halves of that have to be
shown together; showing only the platform-side sentence in front of a `QUOTE_ONLY` election is how a
creator reads a guarantee that was never made to them.

Two boundaries that hold in both modes:

- **Creator assets never enter the platform settlement pipeline.** The platform's route to WETH moves
  the platform's own buckets and nothing else.
- **Creator conversion costs apply only to the creator's own entitlement**, and platform conversion
  costs only to the platform's.

## Secondary-sale royalties, and the one thing that differs by chain

LP fees are one revenue leg; marketplace royalties on secondary sales are the other, and they are a
separate election made at launch.

Most projects want `OPTIONAL`: ERC-2981 advertises a royalty and every marketplace is free to honour
or ignore it, which keeps the token tradeable everywhere. `ENFORCED` adds transfer validation
through a vetted validator, and it narrows where the token can trade. It is never a default and is
never chosen for you.

**If you elect `ENFORCED`, the chain you launch on decides which policy version is correct.**

<!-- generated:creator-earnings -->
<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-doc-assets.mjs. Do not edit inside this block. -->

| Policy version | Validator architecture | Validator address | Chains that resolve it | Default? |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Limit Break CreatorTokenTransferValidator | `0x721C0078c2328597Ca70F5451ffF5A7B38D4E947` | 1, 8453 | **yes** |
| 2 | Limit Break CreatorTokenTransferValidator (modular ruleset) | `0x721C008fdff27BF06E7E123956E2Fe03B63342e3` | 1, 8453 | no |
| 3 | OpenSea StrictAuthorizedTransferSecurityRegistry | `0xA000027A9B2802E1ddf7000061001e5c005A0000` | 4663 | no |

A creator elects a **mode** — `NONE`, `OPTIONAL`, `ENFORCED` — and, for `ENFORCED`, a **policy version**. They never name a validator address; the version resolves one, per chain, against a codehash pinned for that chain.

- Expressing no preference resolves to policy version **1**. The highest version this build knows is **3**; above it the launch reverts `InvalidValidatorPolicyVersion`.
- On a chain where the requested version resolves to nothing, the launch reverts `EnforcedEarningsUnavailableOnChain(chainId, policyVersion)`. **There is no silent downgrade to another version, and no fallback to `OPTIONAL`.**
- Ceiling: **1000 bps**. 10%, the maximum OpenSea documents a collection may set. Configuring above it is rejected outright, never silently clamped.
- `ENFORCED` is unavailable on chain 56. BNB Smart Chain has no vetted validator under any policy version. Presence of Limit Break bytecode at the canonical addresses there is a consequence of permissionless CREATE2 deployment, not a supported-chain announcement, and OpenSea carries no NFT listings or offers on BNB at all. NONE and OPTIONAL remain available on every chain.

A policy version means ONE validator architecture on every chain that resolves it. Versions 1 and 2 are Limit Break CreatorTokenTransferValidator deployments; version 3 is OpenSea's StrictAuthorizedTransferSecurityRegistry, a different contract with a different authorization model. Reusing version 2 for it would have made one label mean two architectures depending on where a creator launched.

<!-- /generated:creator-earnings -->

The practical consequence, stated plainly: **on Ethereum and Base, leave the policy version unset —
the default is right. On Robinhood Chain you must name version 3 explicitly.** The default resolves
to version 1, whose validator has no code at all on Robinhood Chain, and the launch is **refused**
with `EnforcedEarningsUnavailableOnChain(4663, 1)` rather than quietly moved onto a different
validator. A refusal you can read is the correct outcome there — a silent downgrade would put your
collection under an enforcement contract you never chose, and you would find out from a marketplace
rather than from a revert.

Two things this table is not saying. Presence of validator bytecode at an address on some other
chain is a consequence of permissionless CREATE2 deployment, not a supported-chain announcement —
every row above is a deliberate pin backed by a codehash measured on the chain it names. And the
codehash is per-chain even when the address is not: the same validator address holds a different
runtime on Ethereum than on Base, which is exactly why a single chain-invariant pin is impossible.

## What the protocol does not promise

- No price, floor, or return. Genesis liquidity is single-sided: at launch there is executable ask
  liquidity and **no bid depth** until real buyers put quote currency into the pool.
- No revenue if nobody trades. The split is of fees that exist; zero volume is zero fees.
- No control over Uniswap's protocol fee, which is outside this system entirely.
- No project-funded bootstrap buying to manufacture volume or holders. Launch on real trades.

## Custody, stated neutrally

Genesis liquidity is minted directly against the `PoolManager` and held by the immutable liquidity
locker and kernel, not sent to you. The creator receives a **`ProjectRights`** token that carries the
fee entitlement, not the liquidity position — and transferring that token transfers the project,
including its unclaimed and future creator revenue. There is no separate "sell the fee stream"
transaction.

The narrow, true claim is: *genesis liquidity principal is held by the immutable locker and cannot be
withdrawn through the deployed locker.* That is a statement about the locker's bytecode, not about
every risk. The components around it are upgradeable by a 2-of-3 Safe with no timelock, token prices
can fall to nothing, and a creator can behave badly in ways no contract prevents. The guarantee is
narrow because narrow is what is true — see
[11 — Governance and upgradeability](11-governance-and-upgradeability.md).
